title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

The subscription also covers 10 devices at once (so there’s room for your phone, laptop, and TV without switching between them), with apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and supported TV devices, including Fire TV. Whatever device you use, there’s no bandwidth cap to keep track of, though the speed depends on your connection and which of Proton’s 20,000-plus servers you choose—its VPN Accelerator may help, but the advertised improvement of up to 400% applies to VPN connections, and it shouldn’t be read as a promise to quadruple your broadband speed.Beyond changing your apparent location, privacy is the stronger reason to consider Proton, whose apps are open-source and independently audited, with a published external audit of its no-logs policy offering more accountability than a blanket promise of anonymity—but those checks, while useful, won’t stop a website from recognizing you when you sign in. For extra protection (at the possible expense of speed), you can also enable Secure Core, which sends traffic through an additional server in places such as Switzerland or Iceland. Meanwhile, NetShield blocks known ad, tracking, and malware domains, helping prevent some unwanted resources from loading without guaranteeing ad-free streaming or protection against every threat. title: This New iOS 27 Feature May Save You From Getting Scammed
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: LuckyDuck via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams. These scams rely on pressure tactics to trick you into bypassing security features for your phone, laptop, or online accounts. Here's how iOS 27's "Impersonation Risk Detection" works, what it can do, and its current limitations.How Impersonation Risk Detection works to protect you from scamsIn a social engineering scam, a bad actor impersonates an official rep of a bank, government agency, or a tech company such as Apple, Google, or Microsoft. The scammer may even impersonate your friends, family members, or colleagues you trust. They'll try to force you to disable account security measures such as two-factor authentication, or talk you into sharing your financial information. They'll create a fake problem, establish trust, and then pressure you into making large payments. Apple says Impersonation Risk Detection can analyze information about your iPhone or iPad, your Apple Account, and check for signs of an active scam. Once it completes the analysis, iOS 27 will share a risk level with the app that's being targeted by scammers. Apple emphasizes that the app doesn't receive any data associated with your device or Apple Account that was used to assess the risk level.
From there, it's up to the app to decide how to proceed. If an app supports Impersonation Risk Detection, it may add a delay to each step you're trying to execute, show warnings, or even ask you to verify your identity. Apps can use various factors to decide if they need a risk assessment from iOS 27, which include big changes to your account, resetting its password, disabling two-factor authentication, making large payments, etc.What are the various risk levels in Impersonation Risk Detection?Once an app requests iOS 27 for a risk assessment, the operating system can conduct an analysis and place the action into one of three risk level markers (again, Apple doesn't control what apps do with the risk level information):Unknown: This means that iOS 27 couldn't detect any suspicious activity. Apple says that doesn't mean the action was confirmed as safe.Medium: This risk level is assigned when iOS 27 detects some signs of suspicious activity.High: This risk level is associated with significant signs of suspicious activity.How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 (or your iPad to iPadOS 27), go to Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and tap Impersonation Risk Detection. Enable the toggle next to "Share with App Developers." Now, tap Share with App Developers in the pop-up. Once Impersonation Risk Detection is enabled, you don't need to take further action. Note that when you try to disable this feature, it may take up to 24 hours to take effect. This is to protect you from scammers, who may pressure you into disabling the feature.In the same settings page, you'll be able to see which app requested access to your risk levels, and why. This will show up under the "Recent Activity" section. You'll also be able to turn off this feature for individual apps that appear in this section, but, again, it may take up to 24 hours to disable the setting.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The limitations of Impersonation Risk DetectionSecurity features are only as strong as their weakest links. In the case of iOS 27's Impersonation Risk Detection, there are two main weak links. First, this feature is disabled by default. Most people aren't going to dig deep enough into settings to discover it accidentally, and the feature isn't going to be used widely unless people know about it. Second, this feature also depends on app developers adding support for it. Big tech companies and indie developers may adopt it reasonably quickly, but other developers may not rush to implement this feature.There's also the fact that plenty of apps have already spent a lot of resources building up their own security infrastructure, and they may not necessarily see value in adding support for this feature. Here in India, all banking and payment apps show multiple full-screen warnings when you try to make a payment while on a phone call. Some apps may even disable payment features if they detect that a screen-sharing app is installed on your device. So, really, it will come down to how app developers respond to this feature.Does Impersonation Risk Detection keep my data private?Apple says that Impersonation Risk Detection performs its analysis on-device, and that the data used to generate the risk level doesn't leave your device. The company also highlights that the contents of your email, photos, or messages are not analyzed for the risk assessment. When an app requests a risk assessment, Apple claims it only receives information about the type of action you performed in that specific app. Once the risk level is generated, apps don't receive any additional data about you.

title: Here's Why You Should Care About the iPhone 18 Pro's 'Vapor Chambers'
description:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
    Table of Contents
body:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        During Apple’s big hardware announcement on Wednesday, the company placed a particular emphasis on the vapor chamber in the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The glossed-over explanation is that these new vapor chambers can improve performance and reduce heat generation. But how exactly? And what does that mean for the phones you’re planning to buy?How vapor chambers workOn a very simple level, vapor chambers work similarly to liquid cooling in other electronics systems like some desktop PCs or server racks. The goal is to carry heat away from the processor to keep it cool, so it can do more work without overheating. A cooler processor is a more efficient processor, which means it runs better.Except, unlike a PC or server rack, a phone is a tight, compact system. There’s not enough space to heat water and then pump it away to a different location to cool it down. Instead, a vapor chamber is a thin, hollow chamber, typically made of either copper or stainless steel, with a small amount of liquid inside. When the liquid inside heats up, it becomes a gas, which then expands outwards, dispersing the heat throughout the body of your phone, rather than keeping it all close to the processor. As it gets further away from the source of heat, the vapor cools back down and becomes a liquid again.
Since the chamber is sealed, the liquid can’t evaporate and escape, meaning that the fluid can theoretically keep cycling through the chamber indefinitely for the life of the phone. Most manufacturers also pair this with some form of heat sink, like thin sheets of graphite or copper. Or, in the case of the new iPhone 18 Pro, both.Why vapor chambers matter for smartphonesKeeping your phone cool is a massive problem compared to other electronic devices you might have, simply because they’re so small, yet so powerful. A moderately powered laptop like a MacBook Air can get away with a combination of conductive heat sinks, a metal frame, and low heat-generating processors to stay functional, while high-powered gaming laptops have space to stuff in large, laborious fans.Your phone, however, needs to fit in your pocket, and a huge chunk of the space inside needs to be devoted to the battery to make sure it lasts long enough to get through the day. Once you account for all the processors, sensors, and antennas that a phone needs, there’s scarcely any space left for heat dissipation. That’s a huge part of why phones generally don’t have as powerful processors as tablets or laptops. Physically, it’s not impossible to fit a high-powered chip in a pocketable device. But it would likely generate so much heat that it would destroy itself without proper heat dissipation, which would make your phone too big for a pocket.This kind of heat dissipation matters even more if you happen to live in places with warm climates. For example, I live in Texas. Even when driving inside an air-conditioned car, if my phone is in the sunlight, it can start to overheat. When I previously had a Pixel 6 Pro, it would occasionally shut off (taking my navigation with it) simply because it wasn’t in the shade. After upgrading to a Pixel 9 Pro, which does have a vapor chamber, I never noticed this problem—though this is obviously anecdotal.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to consider vapor chambers when buying a phoneApple says the iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the previous generation, which theoretically should mean better cooling and, thus, better performance. But does that mean you need to decide what phone to buy based on how big a phone’s vapor chamber is, or whether it has one at all?Well, yes and no. It turns out that outside the Apple ecosystem, Android phones have been using vapor chambers for years, and you might not have even noticed. The existence of vapor chambers is increasingly becoming standard, so unless you have an old phone that frequently overheats, or you’re looking to buy a phone a few generations behind, you probably don’t need to go out of your way to make sure your phone has one.And whether bigger is necessarily better is also a bit of a gray area. All other things being equal, yes, a larger vapor chamber will dissipate heat better and keep your phone cooler. But all other things are rarely equal. A larger vapor chamber also means the manufacturer can put a more powerful processor inside and achieve the same thermal balance. So, a phone could theoretically be equally likely to overheat, but do more before it does.Figuring out the right balance between processing power and heat dissipation is the kind of thing best left to the engineers and dedicated hobbyists. But there are a couple of things the average person can take away from this. First, if you live in a warm climate, better heat dissipation is always going to be better. Your phone isn’t running at full power all day, but the Texas sun is. So, if you’re worried about your environment causing overheating problems, check phone reviews for how well it handles heat. More importantly, consider the power needs you have for your device before you buy. If you just use your phone to scroll TikTok and reply to emails, you probably don’t need an overpowered processor, but if you plan to edit 4K videos or play graphically intense mobile games, then better thermal regulation could do you some good.
